title: Temitope Oriola: Review of Alberta's police watchdog, Crown prosecutors long overdue
article: The decision to conduct a review of the Alberta Crown Prosecution Service and the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) is a long overdue intervention. Media reports indicate that erstwhile Appeal Court judge Peter Martin has been hired by Justice Minister Mickey Amery to spearhead the process.

I have devoted multiple articles in this column to alert the public and policymakers on the highly problematic nature of some of the decisions made by the Alberta Crown Prosecution Service vis-à-vis cases investigated by ASIRT. I was concerned that the Crown was getting unnecessarily mired in law enforcement politics, which could lead to erosion of trust in criminal justice institutions.

As I noted on Oct. 31, 2024, much of the activities of the Crown is shielded from public view and scrutiny unlike police officers who are arguably the most visible symbol of state power in democratic societies. Therefore, that necessitates a higher threshold of circumspection in decision-making.

ASIRT and similar organizations in Canada rarely recommend charges against police officers for conduct in the line of duty. When they do, the evidence tends to be quite strong and overwhelming to any objective observer. The cases of Steven Nguyen and Pacey Dumas are particularly noteworthy. Nguyen was holding a cellphone when an Edmonton police officer fatally shot him multiple times in June 2021. Dumas was kicked in the head by an Edmonton police officer in December 2020.

In both instances, ASIRT concluded that "there are reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed" but the Crown declined to press charges. The Crown did not provide any public justification for refusing ASIRT's recommendation. Apparently, it does not have to.

The Crown relies on the police to do their job and professional ties are formed. Maintaining such bonds can become a reified objective. That is not unique to Alberta or Canada. However, I cautioned in October against what George F. Cole calls "community game" in his work on the decision-making behind prosecution (or lack thereof). Simply put, the Crown's intervention in ASIRT decisions is unnecessarily and dangerously meddlesome. I was pleased to see that the minister appointed Justice Martin shortly after the October column.

Justice Martin's review will do well to address issues such as the prosecutorial powers of ASIRT, the organization's relationship with the Crown and explicit articulation of the right of the public to know and the rights of victims and their families. The machinery of ASIRT grinds extremely slowly. Cases routinely take three to four years although there appears to be an improvement in recent times. Nonetheless, ASIRT is significantly behind its peers in England and Wales as well as much of Northern Europe.

In 2021, as special adviser to the Government of Alberta on Police Act Review, I offered 14 recommendations regarding police oversight as part of my broader assignment. In one of my submissions, my first recommendation was to have "a single entity for civilian oversight of all police services in Alberta." This would address the current highly fragmented landscape (police commissions, Law Enforcement Review Board, and ASIRT, for instance).

The second recommendation dealt with "Independence of Civilian Oversight" while the fifth focused on the "Range of powers of the proposed independent oversight agency." I believe those recommendations remain relevant today.

Given professional interactions in the criminal justice system in which the Crown and police services are centred, on one hand and the need for independent civilian oversight of the police on the other, ASIRT or any organization of its kind should be allowed to have full investigative and prosecutorial powers with no intervention from any other institution, particularly within the criminal justice system. In some jurisdictions, organizations like ASIRT report directly to the legislature. This will contribute to greater trust and confidence of affected families and the public in the outcome of cases.

I commend Justice Minister Mickey Amery for initiating the review. I have heard nothing but good words about Justice Peter Martin. I wish him good luck on this important assignment. I hope his recommendations are made public and implemented.
Temitope Oriola is professor of criminology at the University of Alberta and recipient of the Gerald L. Gall Human Rights Award.
